Maladaptive Strategies.value: I force myself to think only positive thoughts

Threat.value: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively
Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel isolated and set apart from others
The person I have become is unrecognisable to me
My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe

vignette: Mara, a 58‑year‑old Māori rabbi, recounts the day she was a passenger in a school bus that was suddenly struck by a tree on a foggy morning. The impact slammed her into the back of the vehicle, the glass shattering like a thousand tiny mirrors. When she came to, smoke still curled from the front, a harsh burnt smell clinging to her clothes, and her ears rang with the faint, frantic thud of metal on metal. She remembers the flash of flames that danced along the side of the bus, the searing heat that seemed to melt the air itself, and the terrified shouts of children who had only a second to react before the world turned to black. The memory of that instant lodged itself deep inside her, a constant undercurrent that would later surface whenever the scent of charred wood or the sound of a door slamming too abruptly echoed her mind. After the accident, Mara began to experience night terrors that would wake her in a panic, lungs tight, heart pounding. The nightmares carried the same burnt aroma, and each time she woke, she would find herself covering her face with her hands as though to shield it from an invisible flame. The instinct to hide her face became a coping tactic that she forced herself to repeat when any unexpected touch occurred, turning a brief brush of a coworker’s hand into a startle reaction that left her breathing shallow. These moments of sudden alarm led Mara to forcefully think only of the “good” things in her life—an effort at positive reframing—yet each time the trigger returned she could not help but feel her body reacting as if danger still loomed. The relentless flash of burnt odor, the jarring wake‑ups, and the involuntary covering of her face were all ways in which the triggers sparked threat: an irritability that exploded in brief, angry outbursts at fellow staff, a willingness to take risky shortcuts on the way to the synagogue, and an acute startle to any touch. Her sense of isolation grew in the months after the crash. She felt that the people around her could no longer see the woman she had become; her identity had shifted, leaving her feeling unrecognizable to herself. The isolation, she believed, was a direct result of the threat she perceived—her anger at colleagues, her risky decisions in everyday life, her constant need to cover her face. She convinced herself that she was a danger to those around her, and this reinforced her belief that she must remain alone, which in turn sharpened the memory of that burnt day whenever she encountered a new trigger. The isolation, in turn, intensified the threat she felt whenever she perceived risk, creating a loop where the very belief that she was separated from others fueled her irritability and her sense of bodily menace. When her irritable, risk‑laden moods surged, Mara’s coping mechanisms tightened. In the heat of an argument, she would suddenly overeat, gulping large portions of food in an attempt to soothe the tremor that shivered through her. This overeating, coupled with her insistence on positive thoughts, did little to quench the underlying fear that her body was an enemy, still primed to fight. It also amplified her sense of being unrecognizable—each bite of cake added pounds, each forced smile in front of the congregation felt rehearsed. Her overindulgence and the constant effort to reframe her thoughts began to reinforce her belief that she had lost touch with her authentic self. Moreover, her habit of covering her face whenever a sudden touch happened made her more aware of any tactile stimuli, turning ordinary greetings from students and congregants into potential triggers. The cycle tightened further, as her attempts to suppress threat with maladaptive strategies only fed the negative appraisals that she was isolated and unrecognizable. Today, Mara sits in a small, dimly lit office, her hands trembling as she prepares to write a letter. The burnt smell of the bus’s smoke lingers faintly in the air, and she can hear the echo of a sudden knock on the door. She recognizes the pattern: the trigger, the threat, the maladaptive coping, the negative belief. For months she has avoided the synagogue after work, preferring to remain at home, her face hidden behind the curtain of her kitchen. The decision to finally seek therapy came after a colleague’s remark that she “seemed to have lost her spark,” and Mara could no longer deny that she had become a stranger to her own heart. Her greatest fear now is that if she confronts the cycle, she may lose the very identity that kept her community together; her greatest hope is to reclaim the calm that once allowed her to guide her congregation through difficult times.
